results.name: singleton_set_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate on sets with exactly one example, for targets other than that example; observed above null means the model under-generalizes from a single example (size principle too sharp), below null means it over-generalizes.

results.name: proximity_slope
results.description: OLS slope of the yes response on distance (1-15) from the target to the nearest example, excluding targets that are examples; more negative observed than null means people's similarity gradient is steeper than the model's, less negative means the model's falloff is too steep.
results.code:
# name: proximity_slope
# description: OLS slope of the yes response on distance (1-15) from the target to the nearest example, excluding targets that are examples; more negative observed than null means people's similarity gradient is steeper than the model's, less negative means the model's falloff is too steep.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    m = (d >= 1) & (d <= 15)
    if m.sum() < 3:
        return 0.0
    x = d[m]
    y = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)[m]
    xc = x - x.mean()
    v = (xc ** 2).sum()
    if v == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float((xc * (y - y.mean())).sum() / v)

results.name: shared_last_digit_advantage
results.description: Among non-example targets with the same parity as at least one example, yes rate for targets sharing a final digit with some example minus yes rate for those that do not; observed above null means the model under-weights final-digit similarity, below null means it over-weights it.
results.code:
# name: shared_last_digit_advantage
# description: Among non-example targets with the same parity as at least one example, yes rate for targets sharing a final digit with some example minus yes rate for those that do not; observed above null means the model under-weights final-digit similarity, below null means it over-weights it.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    is_ex = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    same_par = np.any(np.mod(ex, 2) == np.mod(t, 2)[:, None], axis=1)
    share = np.any(np.mod(ex, 10) == np.mod(t, 10)[:, None], axis=1)
    y = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    base = (~is_ex) & same_par
    a = base & share
    b = base & ~share
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: cluster_interior_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate to non-example targets strictly inside the span of the examples, on sets of >=2 examples spanning at most 20; observed above null means the model under-produces "yes" inside tight clusters (people treat them as ranges more than the model), below null means it over-produces them.
results.code:
# name: cluster_interior_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate to non-example targets strictly inside the span of the examples, on sets of >=2 examples spanning at most 20; observed above null means the model under-produces "yes" inside tight clusters (people treat them as ranges more than the model), below null means it over-produces them.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)
    hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    is_ex = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    m = (n >= 2) & (hi - lo <= 20) & (t > lo) & (t < hi) & ~is_ex
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].to_numpy()[m].mean())

results.name: even_target_yes_after_all_odd_sets
results.description: Yes rate to even targets on sets of >=2 examples that are all odd; observed above null means the model under-produces "yes" to parity-violating targets (people are less sure of the "odd" rule / noisier than the model), below null means it over-produces them.
results.code:
# name: even_target_yes_after_all_odd_sets
# description: Yes rate to even targets on sets of >=2 examples that are all odd; observed above null means the model under-produces "yes" to parity-violating targets (people are less sure of the "odd" rule / noisier than the model), below null means it over-produces them.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    all_odd = np.all(np.isnan(ex) | (np.mod(ex, 2) == 1), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    m = (n >= 2) & all_odd & (t % 2 == 0)
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].to_numpy()[m].mean())

results.name: cell_response_extremity
results.description: Mean over (set, target) cells of |cell yes rate - 0.5|; observed below null means the model's predictions are over-confident (too close to 0/1, lacking a lapse/noise component), above null means people are more deterministic than the model.

results.name: far_target_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate to targets more than 20 away from the nearest example, on sets of >=2 examples; observed above null means the model generalizes too little far from the examples (too range-bound), below null means it generalizes too much.
results.code:
# name: far_target_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate to targets more than 20 away from the nearest example, on sets of >=2 examples; observed above null means the model generalizes too little far from the examples (too range-bound), below null means it generalizes too much.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    m = (n >= 2) & (d > 20)
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].to_numpy()[m].mean())

results.name: trial_index_yes_correlation
results.description: Pearson correlation between trial_index and the yes response; observed more negative than null means people say "yes" less as the session goes on (a drift the stationary model does not produce), more positive means the reverse.
